<style>
  :root{
    /* Canonical brand tokens — PlotNua Brand Package v1.0. Do not alter. */
    --brand-green:#1F3B2E; --brand-ivory:#F2EFE6; --brand-sage:#8FAF8A;
    --cream:#F2EFE6; --paper:#F8F5EC; --ink:#1F3B2E; --soft:#55605A;
    --accent:#4F6B4A; --oak:#8B6F4E;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box; margin:0; padding:0;}
  html{scroll-behavior:smooth;}
  body{ font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; background:var(--paper); color:var(--ink); overflow-x:hidden; }
  h1,h2,h3{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-weight:600; letter-spacing:-.01em; }
  h1,h2{ font-weight:700; }

  .reveal{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(6px); transition:opacity 1.1s ease, transform 1.1s ease; }
  .reveal.in{ opacity:1; transform:none; }

  /* ---- fixed brand mark (unchanged from Brand Integration v1) ---- */
  .brand-mark{
    position:fixed; top:22px; left:22px; z-index:50;
    display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;
    width:46px; height:46px; padding:0;
    background:var(--brand-ivory);
    border-radius:12px;
    box-shadow:0 1px 3px rgba(31,59,46,.16), 0 0 0 1px rgba(31,59,46,.07);
    opacity:0; transition:opacity 1.6s ease, transform .4s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1), box-shadow .4s ease;
    text-decoration:none;
  }
  .brand-mark:hover{ transform:scale(1.06); box-shadow:0 5px 16px rgba(31,59,46,.20), 0 0 0 1px rgba(31,59,46,.09); }

  /* RESULTS-003 PART D — THE FLOATING BACK.
     Identical to the control on Results and My Plot: same corner, same 44px
     minimum height, same radius, paper ground, hairline border and shadow,
     same type. Only the label and destination differ, because they must.

     It does not fight the brand mark. Measured: .brand-mark is fixed at
     TOP:22px left:22px, this is fixed at BOTTOM:22px left:22px. Opposite
     ends of the screen at every viewport. (I twice deferred this work on the
     stated grounds that they shared a corner. They never did.)

     z-index 60 sits above the page and below .am-modal-overlay (200), so an
     open modal covers it rather than having it float over a dialog. */
  .pn-return{
    position:fixed; left:22px; bottom:22px; z-index:60;
    display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:8px;
    min-height:44px; padding:11px 17px 11px 14px;
    background:var(--paper, #F8F5EC); color:var(--ink, #1F3B2E);
    border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.16); border-radius:24px;
    box-shadow:0 2px 10px rgba(31,59,46,.13);
    font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:14px; font-weight:500;
    text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer;
    -webkit-appearance:none; appearance:none;
  }
  .pn-return:hover{ border-color:rgba(31,59,46,.3); }
  .pn-return-arrow{ font-size:15px; line-height:1; }
  @media (max-width:600px){
    .pn-return{ left:16px; bottom:16px; padding:10px 15px 10px 12px; font-size:13.5px; }
  }
  .brand-mark.in{ opacity:1; }
  .brand-mark img{ display:block; width:34px; height:34px; border-radius:8px; }
  @media(max-width:720px){
    .brand-mark{ top:16px; left:16px; width:40px; height:40px; }
    .brand-mark img{ width:30px; height:30px; }
  }

  /* ================= DISCOVERY — HERO =================
     Same visual grammar as the About page hero: a single still image,
     bottom-anchored copy, warm ivory serif type. This is the master
     template every future Discovery reuses, so the hero deliberately
     stays close to the About page's pattern rather than inventing a
     new one — consistency here is what makes the site feel like one
     continuous place, not a stitched-together set of templates. */
  .d-hero{ position:relative; width:100%; height:88vh; height:88svh; min-height:540px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink); }
  .d-hero img{
    width:100%; height:100%; object-fit:cover; display:block;
    transform:scale(1.03); opacity:0;
    transition:opacity 1.8s ease-out, transform 6s cubic-bezier(.22,.61,.36,1);
  }
  .d-hero img.on{ opacity:1; transform:scale(1); }
  .d-hero-scrim{ position:absolute; inset:0;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(15,14,10,.14) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,0) 32%, rgba(15,14,10,.10) 60%, rgba(15,14,10,.60) 100%); }
  .d-hero-scrim{ background:linear-gradient(180deg,
    rgba(15,14,10,.16) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,0) 26%,
    rgba(15,14,10,.42) 58%, rgba(15,14,10,.78) 100%); }
  .d-hero-copy{ position:absolute; z-index:2; inset:auto 0 0 0; padding:0 8vw 10vh; text-align:center; }
  /* HERO EYEBROW — ADAPTIVE COLOUR (Master Standard).
     The eyebrow is an orientation label, not a brand element. On this hero
     --brand-sage (luminance 0.36) sat inside the luminance range of the
     plaster wall behind it (0.32-0.49) and washed out; no shadow can
     separate a colour from a background it matches in lightness.
     It therefore uses the same --brand-ivory as h1 / .subtitle / .intro,
     with the same shadow family as .intro. Font, size, weight, tracking
     and position are unchanged. */
  .d-hero-copy .eyebrow{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease, transform 1s ease;
    font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.18em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--brand-ivory); margin-bottom:20px;
    text-shadow:0 1px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.28); }
  .d-hero-copy h1{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .1s, transform 1s ease .1s;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(32px,5vw,58px); line-height:1.14; text-shadow:0 2px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.32); }
  .d-hero-copy .subtitle{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .18s, transform 1s ease .18s;
    margin:18px auto 0; max-width:32ch; font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(16px,1.9vw,21px); line-height:1.55; text-shadow:0 1px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.3); }
  .d-hero-copy .intro{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .26s, transform 1s ease .26s;
    margin:24px auto 0; max-width:50ch; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-weight:300;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(14px,1.4vw,16px); line-height:1.75; text-shadow:0 1px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.28); }
  /* Garden-room search focus (26 Oct 2026): the topic leads the H1;
     the Discovery question remains as its secondary line. */
  .d-hero-copy h1 .d-h1-sub{ display:block; margin:16px auto 0; max-width:40ch; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif;
    font-weight:500; font-size:clamp(11px,1.15vw,13px); line-height:1.6; letter-spacing:.16em; text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); text-shadow:0 1px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.4); }
  .d-hero-copy.in .eyebrow, .d-hero-copy.in h1, .d-hero-copy.in .subtitle{ opacity:1; transform:none; }
  .d-hero-copy.in .intro{ opacity:.86; transform:none; }

  /* Bounded maker comparison: text-only, using the existing page palette. */
  .gr-compare-wrap{max-width:100%;overflow-x:auto;margin:28px 0 0;}
  .gr-compare{width:100%;min-width:580px;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px;line-height:1.65;color:var(--soft);}
  .gr-compare caption{text-align:left;font-size:13px;line-height:1.6;padding-bottom:16px;}
  .gr-compare th,.gr-compare td{text-align:left;vertical-align:top;padding:18px 16px;border-bottom:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.16);}
  .gr-compare thead th{color:var(--accent);font-weight:600;}
  .gr-compare tbody th{width:25%;font-weight:500;}
  .gr-compare th:first-child,.gr-compare td:first-child{padding-left:0;}

  /* ================= ARTICLE RHYTHM (shared with About) ================= */
  .article{ max-width:1040px; margin:0 auto; padding:0 7vw; }
  .article-section{ padding:9.5vh 0; border-bottom:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.06); }
  .article-section:last-of-type{ border-bottom:none; }
  .article-section .kicker{ font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.16em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--accent); margin-bottom:19px; }
  .article-section h2{ font-size:clamp(26px,3.4vw,40px); line-height:1.32; max-width:19ch; margin-bottom:26px; }
  .article-section p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:17px; line-height:1.85; max-width:60ch; }
  .article-section p + p{ margin-top:20px; }

  /* ---- The Spark — the emotional opening line of every Discovery.
     Deliberately the quietest, largest moment on the page: one
     sentence, generous whitespace, nothing else competing with it. ---- */
  .spark{ position:relative; padding:12vh 7vw; text-align:center; background:var(--paper); overflow:hidden; }
  .spark::before{ content:''; position:absolute; top:0; left:0; right:0; height:16vh;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(20,26,20,.05) 0%, rgba(20,26,20,0) 100%); pointer-events:none; }
  .spark p{ position:relative; font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400; color:var(--ink);
    font-size:clamp(25px,3.6vw,40px); line-height:1.5; max-width:21ch; margin:0 auto; letter-spacing:-.005em; }

  /* ---- Imagine Your Property — a second full-width photograph with
     minimal text; this is a mood beat, not an information beat. ---- */
  .imagine-photo{ position:relative; width:100%; height:84vh; height:84svh; min-height:460px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink); }
  .imagine-photo img{ width:100%; height:100%; object-fit:cover; display:block; }
  .imagine-photo::before, .imagine-photo::after{ content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; height:5vh; z-index:2; pointer-events:none; }
  .imagine-photo::before{ top:0; background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(248,245,236,.5) 0%, rgba(248,245,236,0) 100%); }
  .imagine-photo::after{ bottom:0; background:linear-gradient(0deg, rgba(242,239,230,.5) 0%, rgba(242,239,230,0) 100%); }
  .imagine-photo .caption{ position:absolute; z-index:3; left:0; right:0; bottom:0; padding:7vh 8vw;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(15,14,10,0) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,.42) 100%); text-align:center; }
  .imagine-photo .caption p{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(16px,1.85vw,20px); max-width:32ch; margin:0 auto; text-shadow:0 1px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.3); letter-spacing:.01em; }

  /* ---- Understanding the Opportunity — practical detail, still

  .partners .article{ position:relative; z-index:1; padding-top:12vh; padding-bottom:12vh; text-align:center; }

  .partners p{ margin:0 auto; max-width:52ch; }
  .partners .partner-frame{ margin:48px auto 0; max-width:420px; padding:38px 32px; border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.10); border-radius:2px; }
  .partners .partner-frame p{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; color:var(--accent); font-size:16px; line-height:1.75; max-width:none; }

  /* ---- inline links in body copy, carried from the launch standard ---- */
  .article-section p a, .planning-conditions a, .faq-a a, .rule-note a{
    color:var(--accent); text-decoration:none;
    border-bottom:1px solid rgba(79,107,74,.35); padding-bottom:1px;
    transition:border-color .3s ease; }
  .article-section p a:hover, .planning-conditions a:hover, .faq-a a:hover,
  .rule-note a:hover{
    border-bottom-color:var(--accent); }

  /* ---- hand-off pair, as DISC-004 ---- */
  .handoff-pair{ margin-top:30px; display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:14px; }
  .handoff{ padding:22px 26px 24px; background:var(--cream);

  .handoff p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:15.5px; line-height:1.7; max-width:52ch; margin:0 0 12px; }

/* ---- THE OPENING IS THE COMPARISON.
     #gardenCompare now lives inside .d-hero. The component itself is
     unchanged — every .cmp rule above still applies to it. These four rules
     do only two things: make it fill the hero instead of standing as its own
     mid-page plate, and stop the hero's single-photograph entrance animation
     (opacity 0 -> 1, scale 1.03 -> 1 over six seconds) from being applied to
     two clipped plates, which would have faded the whole comparison in and
     slid one plate against the other.

     The scrim and the copy are made pointer-transparent because they cover
     the frame: without that, a drag started anywhere in the hero would land
     on them and the slider would only respond in the strip between. ---- */
  
  
  
  .d-hero .d-hero-scrim{ z-index:3; pointer-events:none; }
  .d-hero .d-hero-copy{ z-index:7; pointer-events:none; }

  /* ---- THE RULE CARDS.
     Eighteen statutory conditions in four groups. They were one vertical run
     of dotted bullets — accurate, and indistinguishable from a government
     notice. The facts are byte-identical; only the frame is new, and it is
     built from the Results dossier's vocabulary: a hairline, a small accent
     label, and TWO levels of type inside each condition, so the fact reads
     first and its qualifier reads second instead of every clause carrying
     the same weight. ---- */
  .rule-cards{ list-style:none; padding:0; margin:26px 0 0;
    display:grid; gap:16px; grid-template-columns:repeat(2,1fr); }
  .rule-cards > li{ margin:0; }
  .rule-card{ height:100%; background:var(--paper);
    border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.14); border-radius:4px;
    padding:22px 24px 20px; }
  .rule-card > h3{ font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:11px; font-weight:500;
    letter-spacing:.15em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--accent);
    margin:0 0 14px; }
  .rule-list{ list-style:none; padding:0; margin:0; }
  .rule-list > li{ padding:11px 0; border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.09); }
  .rule-list > li:first-child{ padding-top:0; border-top:none; }
  .rule-list > li:last-child{ padding-bottom:0; }
  .rule-fact{ display:block; font-size:15px; line-height:1.45; font-weight:600;
    color:var(--ink); }
  .rule-note{ display:block; margin-top:4px; font-size:13.5px; line-height:1.6;
    color:var(--soft); }

     hairline, smaller type. Present, findable, and visibly not one of the
     four principal groups. ---- */

    letter-spacing:.15em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--soft);
    margin:34px 0 12px; }
  .check-rows{ list-style:none; padding:0; margin:0;

blocks: Comparing garden rooms in Ireland?

A garden room can give you a separate place to work, make art, exercise or spend time together. PlotNua brings the makers, pricing questions and planning conditions into one guide, so you can compare your options before asking for a quote.

Start with the use, then compare the complete project: the building, its insulation and glazing, delivery, installation, foundations, VAT and connections. A garden office used every working day and a weekend studio need different specifications. If somebody will live there, follow the separate garden-home guidance below.
Looking for makers? Explore garden room and garden office makers , then check the product details and the availability information for each option.

Working out a budget? The garden room prices guide separates published prices by what they cover. Use its checklist to ask about foundations, installation, VAT and electrical connection before comparing quotes.
Checking your garden? Read the planning conditions below and use the property check on this page. The conditions matter as much as the size of the building.
Choosing a garden office for everyday use

Ask the maker to explain the insulation in the floor, walls and roof, the glazing, ventilation and heating, and what is included in the quoted price. Think about where your desk will go, daylight on the screen, sockets and an internet connection. Ask how the building will reach your garden and whether the quote allows for your site.

For a closer look at one construction system, read about the TRIQ QUBE solid-timber garden office . Its published price is for the German market, not an Irish delivered price. Delivery to an Irish address needs individual confirmation from the manufacturer; installation in Ireland has not been established.
Compare garden room makers and specifications.

These three researched examples show why the headline price needs a closer look. They are a starting point, not a ranking of suppliers or a complete market comparison. Open each guide for the published prices, source links and questions to take to the maker.
Two researched examples. Each guide identifies its sources and check date.
Maker and range

All In One Cabins: Boderg, Corry and Kilglass
Flatpack single-room cabins. Wall thickness alone does not establish thermal performance.
Starting prices; VAT needs confirmation. Installation is described separately, so confirm the complete site quotation. The Corry has conflicting size information.
Concept Modular garden offices
Standard and Signature offices, with different interior fit-outs.
Published prices exclude VAT, base pads, installation, craneage and haulage. Electricity connection is separately priced.
Shomera garden rooms: Classic and Contemporary
Timber-frame garden studios; Contemporary designs add overhangs and recessed outdoor space.
Product pages include build and installation in starting prices. Confirm VAT, decoration, landscaping and the final site-specific scope.

For each route, confirm delivery to your address, access, the agreed specification and the final price in writing. A published listing is not a site assessment or a finding that the building is exempt from planning.

Since 27 July 2026, two different buildings can go at the end of an Irish back garden without a planning application, if the conditions are met. A garden room of up to 30 m² — an office, studio or gym where nobody sleeps. And, new in 2026, a detached garden home of 32 to 45 m² that somebody can live in, with two notices to file and a window that closes at the end of 2030. The Building Regulations keep their own, separate 25 m² threshold. Below: what changed, what counts towards each limit, and how to check your own garden. Thinking of a sauna or a hot tub instead? Garden Retreat covers how the same rules read for each.
Comparing prices? Read PlotNua’s guide to garden room prices in Ireland → Published ranges grouped by what each price covers, and a quote checklist.
What if the room you need is already inside the property line?
Most of us measure the house. When its rooms run out, we think about the house again.
Every room already has a job.
A flat corner at the far end of the garden. Already yours, already level, with nothing on it. Ground is the one thing a full house cannot make more of.
A building there stands on its own. Nothing about the house has to change.
Ready to check your garden?
See what may be possible at your address now.
What are you considering?
A home Somebody will live there. The residential conditions apply.
A room A garden office, studio, kids’ space, extra room, gym or other non-residential garden space.
Nothing is bought or reserved here. This is an early property check, not planning permission.
One building. Very different lives.
What changes is not the building. It is what you need it for.
Somewhere to work Thirty steps to work. A garden office, a desk, a room to make things in. A door that closes.
Somewhere for the family to spread into Loud enough to be theirs. Close enough to still be home. Teenagers, music, somewhere that is not the kitchen.

Somewhere for somebody to live An adult child who cannot afford to move out. A parent who would rather be near than far. This one is new. Until 2026 it was the single thing a garden building could not do.
The building does not decide what happens inside it.
Tonight it belongs to the teenagers. Tomorrow it could be anything.
Since July 2026, somebody can live in it.

For years a garden building could be anything except somewhere to sleep. That is what the 2026 regulations changed. Since 27 July 2026 a detached home of 32 to 45 m² can be built in the rear garden of a principal house as exempted development — no planning application, and a set of conditions instead.

The exemption is temporary. It has applied since 27 July 2026, when the regulations came into operation, and closes on 31 December 2030 — and the work has to be both started and finished inside that window. (The regulations count the period from 16 July 2026, the day they were signed.)
A garden room and a garden home are not the same project.
Which rules apply comes down to one question: will anybody sleep there?

A garden room Up to 30 m², and nobody sleeps there. The older garden-structure exemption, raised from 25 m² to 30 m² in July 2026, counting everything already built under it. No notice to the council. Human habitation is expressly excluded, and the use must be incidental to the enjoyment of the house — a home office or a gym, not premises.

A garden home At least 32 m², and somebody can live there. The new exemption. At least 32 m², and no more than 45 m² counting anything already built under the garden-structure exemption. It may only be occupied in conjunction with the main house, and cannot be sold or subdivided.

Two different limits, and only one of them moved. Thirty square metres is the planning ceiling for a garden room. The Building Regulations have their own, separate threshold, and it is still 25 m²: a detached garden building of no more than 25 m² can fall inside the Building Regulations exemption, but only if it also meets the rest of the conditions attached to it — detached from any other building, inside the height limits, and used only for recreation or storage, not for human habitation and not for a trade or business. Go over 25 m², or fail one of those conditions, and the Building Regulations apply to the building in full: structure, fire, ventilation, insulation. You still need no planning application. That is a different question from whether the building has to be built to standard.

The same July 2026 regulations also raised what you can add to the back of the house without permission, from 40 m² to 45 m². If the room you need could be an extension instead, that number moved too.
Could your garden do this?
Five things decide it, and a tape measure settles all five in an evening.
What the house has to keep. 25 m² of private open space must stay for the main house — 5 m by 5 m, say. On a small garden this is the one that decides it, so pace it first.
What the building takes. At least 32 m² for a home: roughly 5.7 m square, before the gap around it.
What is already out there. Anything built under the garden-structure exemption counts against a 45 m² ceiling — more than about 13 m² and the minimum is out of reach.
How close to the wall. The planning minimum is 0.6 m from a wall or boundary. But below 1 m the fire-safety requirements tighten sharply and very little window area is allowed on that side.
Getting to it. A way in on foot or by wheelchair, inside your own property. No new entrance onto the road.

How you measure it. The regulations set the limits in square metres and never say how to measure them. They define “gross floor space” as an internal measurement, but the garden-building rules do not use that term — they say “total area”, which is defined nowhere. That is why a council and a supplier can give you different answers and both point at the text. Measure inside and out, take the larger figure, and if you are within a metre or two of the limit, ask the council before you order.
If those come out in your favour, the next question is your own address.
Two notices, not one.
Exempted development means no planning application. For a garden home, it does not mean nothing to file.
Tell the planning authority, at least 14 days before work starts. The notice gives the location, the Eircode and the reason.
Separately, tell Building Control. A Commencement Notice with Additional Documentation, naming a competent builder and an assigned certifier.

And at the end of it, a Certificate of Compliance on Completion has to be registered by the Building Control Authority before anybody can move in. That is the real finish line, and it is worth knowing at the start.
Garden room prices are hard to compare.
Before you can tell whether one garden room is dearer than another, you have to know what each price covers. Most of the time, it is not published.

245 garden-room products with a euro price we can stand behind. From 24 suppliers, out of 570 garden-room products in PlotNua’s 7 October 2026 research snapshot, corrected on 20 October 2026 for five supplier records, corrected on 26 October 2026 for 59 supplier records, seven base prices rechecked on 26 October 2026.

177 of them do not establish what the price includes. A kit you assemble, a building delivered and erected, and a turnkey finish with foundations and power are three different purchases. The same building lands at very different numbers depending on which one you are being quoted.
92 do not publish whether VAT is in the price. That can make a substantial difference to the price you actually pay.
Only 43 publish a floor area. Which is the one number the planning rules actually turn on.

So we are not going to tell you what a garden room costs in Ireland, and we are certainly not going to tell you what a garden home costs: the market has not published enough for anyone to say honestly. What we can tell you is what to ask.

Before comparing two prices, get the same three answers from both suppliers. Is erection included? Are foundations included? Is VAT included? If the answers differ, the prices were never comparable in the first place.
